title: Pasta e Fagioli
subtitle: Italian rustic pasta and bean soup
excerpt: The most nourishing of Italian soups: a thick, hearty broth of cannellini beans and small pasta, with rosemary, garlic, and tomato, that blurs the line between soup and pasta dish. Thick, starchy, and deeply comforting.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pasta e fagioli (pasta and beans) is one of the defining dishes of cucina povera, the Italian tradition of cheap, nourishing food made from simple ingredients. It is eaten throughout Italy but is particularly associated with Veneto, Campania, and Lazio, each with its regional variation. The Veneto version uses borlotti beans and sometimes includes smoked pork; the Neapolitan version uses mixed pasta scraps and tomato; the Roman version is thick and dense, almost a porridge. All share the technique of cooking some of the beans until they can be mashed, thickening the starchy broth, while leaving others whole for texture. The pasta is cooked directly in the bean liquid, which makes the soup starchier and more cohesive.

content.text: Mash or blend roughly a third of the beans before adding to thicken the soup. Cook the pasta directly in the soup, not separately; it absorbs the starchy liquid and the result is much richer. The soup thickens considerably as it stands; add a little water or stock when reheating.

items.preparation: small pasta: ditalini, small elbows, or broken spaghetti

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrot, and celery for 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, rosemary, chilli flakes, and bay leaves and cook for 2 minutes. Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 3 minutes.
Mash roughly a third of the beans. Add all the beans (mashed and whole) and 1.2 litres of water. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.

Add the pasta directly to the soup. Cook for the pasta packet time, stirring often as the pasta will stick on the bottom. The soup should be very thick; add a little hot water if it gets too stiff. Remove the bay leaves. Serve in deep bowls with a generous pour of extra-virgin olive oil and plenty of black pepper.
